content:
You have a remodel in mind. A kitchen, a bathroom, maybe a full interior overhaul. Now comes the question that decides whether the project goes smoothly or turns into a headache: do you call a handyman or a general contractor.

We get this question constantly, and the honest answer depends on scope, not price. Below is exactly how to tell the difference before you sign anything.

What a Handyman Actually Does Well

A handyman is excellent at small, contained tasks. Fixing a leaky faucet, patching drywall, hanging a door, replacing a light fixture. These are single skill jobs with low risk if something goes wrong.

The problem starts when a homeowner asks a handyman to take on work that involves multiple trades, structural changes, or anything requiring a permit. That is not a knock on handymen. It is simply outside the scope of what the role is built for.

What a General Contractor Is Built to Handle

A licensed general contractor manages the entire project: design, permitting, multiple trades, inspections, and final sign off. This matters most when your remodel touches more than one system in your home.

Structural Changes

Moving a wall, expanding a room, or altering the roofline requires engineering review and a permit. A handyman is not licensed to pull these permits, and skipping this step can affect your home insurance and resale value later.

Multiple Trades in One Project

A kitchen remodel usually touches plumbing, electrical, and carpentry at once. A general contractor coordinates all three under one schedule. A handyman working alone means you are the one coordinating three separate people, three separate timelines, and three separate invoices.

Permit and Code Compliance

Any remodel involving new wiring, plumbing relocation, or structural work needs inspection sign off. A licensed contractor builds this into the project timeline from day one, so you are not caught unprepared when an inspector asks for paperwork that does not exist.

The Real Risk of Choosing Wrong

Here is what most homeowners do not think about until it is too late. If unpermitted or unlicensed work causes damage later, your homeowners insurance may deny the claim entirely.

We have seen firsthand how a low upfront quote from an unlicensed handyman turns into a five figure problem during a home sale, when an inspector flags work that was never permitted. The buyer's lender will not close on a home with unresolved permit issues, and now the seller is paying to fix a problem that should never have existed.

A Simple Way to Decide

Ask yourself one question before hiring anyone: does this project involve more than one trade, a permit, or a structural change. If the answer is yes to any of these, you need a licensed general contractor, not a handyman.

  • Single task, no permit needed, one trade involved: a handyman is often the right call
  • Multiple trades working together on one timeline: you need a general contractor
  • Any structural change or new plumbing and electrical work: a general contractor is required by law
  • A project that affects your home's resale value or insurance standing: always use a licensed contractor
  • Uncertain about scope: ask for a written assessment before hiring anyone

A licensed remodeling services team should be able to tell you within one site visit which category your project falls into.

A Real Remodel, Start to Finish

A homeowner in Tampa hired a handyman to update a kitchen, expecting a quick job. Once demolition began, the handyman discovered the electrical panel could not support new appliance circuits, and the plumbing needed relocation to match the new layout.

The project stalled for weeks while the homeowner searched for licensed help to finish what had already been started. We stepped in, secured the proper permits, coordinated the electrical and plumbing work under one schedule, and completed the remodel with full inspection sign off. What should have taken six weeks took eleven, purely because the wrong professional was hired at the start.

What to Ask Before You Hire Anyone

I always advise clients to ask three questions before signing a contract for any remodel, regardless of size.

Are you licensed and insured for this type of work. Will this project require a permit, and will you handle that process. Who is responsible if something goes wrong during construction. If a handyman cannot give you clear answers to all three, that is your signal to call a general contractor instead.

How One Licensed Team Simplifies Everything

I prioritize a strategy where one team handles design, permitting, and construction under a single contract. This removes the coordination burden from the homeowner entirely, because there is one point of contact accountable for the full project.

Our build services team works alongside remodeling projects specifically to catch structural or code issues before demolition begins, not after. That single decision prevents the exact scenario described above, where a project stalls midway because nobody checked the scope first.

If you are still deciding between fixing small issues yourself and starting a full remodel, our earlier guide on room addition costs breaks down how project scope changes your budget. And if a recent storm is part of what is driving your remodel, our guide on what to do after a tree falls on your roof covers the emergency steps first.

Final Thoughts

A handyman and a general contractor both have a place, but choosing wrong costs far more than the initial quote suggests. If your remodel touches more than one trade, needs a permit, or changes your home's structure, hire a licensed general contractor from the start. It is the difference between one accountable team and a project nobody fully owns.

faqs.q: Can a handyman legally do electrical or plumbing work?
faqs.a: In most cases, no. Electrical and plumbing work typically requires a licensed tradesperson and a permit, which falls outside standard handyman licensing.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to hire a handyman than a general contractor?
faqs.a: For small, single trade tasks, yes. For anything involving multiple trades or structural work, an unlicensed handyman often ends up costing more once permit and rework issues surface.

faqs.q: What happens if I use unpermitted work on a remodel?
faqs.a: Unpermitted work can affect your homeowners insurance and delay or block a home sale later, since lenders often require resolved permits before closing.

faqs.q: How do I know if my remodel needs a permit?
faqs.a: Any project involving structural changes, new electrical circuits, or plumbing relocation almost always requires a permit. A licensed contractor can confirm this during an initial site visit.

faqs.q: Should I hire separate people for each trade in my remodel?
faqs.a: It is not recommended. Coordinating multiple separate contractors increases scheduling conflicts and removes single point accountability if something goes wrong.
